questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
{x}^{2}-1=(x-1)(x+1).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{(x+1)}+\frac{B}{(x-1)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
1=A(x-1)+B(x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A(1-1)+B(1+1) \\ 1 & =2B \\ B & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A(-1-1)+B(-1+1) \\ 1 & =-2A \\ A & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}=-\frac{1}{2(x+1)}+\frac{1}{2(x-1)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{1}{2(x+1)}+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-1}{x+1}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{x-1}{x+1}|{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
4{x}^{2}+5x+1=(4x+1)(x+1).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+1}{4{x}^{2}+5x+1} & =\frac{2x+1}{(4x+1)(x+1)}=\frac{A}{4x+1}+\frac{B}{x+1},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x+1=A(x+1)+B(4x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-1)+1 & =A(-1+1)+B(4(-1)+1) \\ -1 & =-3B \\ B & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{4},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-\frac{1}{4})+1 & =A(-\frac{1}{4}+1)+B(4(-\frac{1}{4})+1) \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{3}{4}A \\ A & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2x+1}{4{x}^{2}+5x+1}=\frac{2}{3(4x+1)}+\frac{1}{3(x+1)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+1}{4{x}^{2}+5x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{3(4x+1)}+\frac{1}{3(x+1)})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{4}{4x+1}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x+1|+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+1}{4{x}^{2}+5x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x+1|+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{4x+1}+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+1)\sqrt{4x+1}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2x+1}{4{x}^{2}+5x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+1)\sqrt{4x+1}|{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\sqrt{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x-4=A(x-4)+Bx.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(4)-4 & =A(4-4)+B(4) \\ 4 & =4B \\ 1 & =B\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-4 & =A(0-4)+B(0) \\ -4 & =-4A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)} & =\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x-4}{x(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\int \frac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)}\,\text{d}x=a\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+b\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C,
$$

find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)} & =\frac{A}{x-3}+\frac{B}{x+3},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
x+15=A(x+3)+B(x-3).
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3+15 & =A(-3+3)+B(-3-3) \\ 12 & =-6B \\ B & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3+15 & =A(3+3)+B(3-3) \\ 18 & =6A \\ A & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)} & =\frac{3}{x-3}-\frac{2}{x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+15}{(x-3)(x+3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x-3}-\frac{2}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{3}{x-3}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{2}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=3,b=-2,$ and $a+b=3-2=1.$
